newsitem.title: USA: CBOT will go to court if CFTC axes corn/soy plan.
newsitem.headline: CBOT will go to court if CFTC axes corn/soy plan.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade will take immediate legal action if the Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not approve a plan to change the corn and soybean delivery system, CBOT Chairman Pat Arbor said.

In an interview on Thursday following the chairman's mid-year address, Arbor told Reuters he expected a CFTC ruling on the proposal by next month and would "litigate immediately" if the decision went against the exchange.
The proposal, approved by the CBOT membership in April by a two-to-one margin, sets delivery points along the Illinois River from Pekin, Ill. to Chicago, and at Burns Harbor, Ind.
The plan also calls for eliminating St. Louis and Toledo as delivery sites, a sticky issue that has landed the exchange in a turf battle with the CFTC.
CFTC has not decided whether to approve the plan but officials in May warned that the clash could end up in court if the two sides could not agree on delivery terms.

The exchange drew up the proposal after the regulatory agency in December told the CBOT that delivery terms of its corn and soybean contracts were no longer suitable due to dwindling warehouse capacity.

But the proposal sparked controversy across the Corn Belt and the debate quickly spread to Washington. CFTC received a record number of letters, largely against the plan, from eastern Corn Belt merchants, producers and politicians who objected to dropping Toledo as a delivery point.
Other opponents have said the plan places unfair emphasis on export channels and could create market manipulation.

The most recent objections came from Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) and 16 other lawmakers who last week asked Attorney General Janet Reno to investigate alleged anti-competitive impacts of the CBOT recommendation.

Arbor said he had not heard from the Justice Department but said accusations of anti-competitiveness were unfounded. He said Kaptur, who represents Toledo, and other politicians were trying to protect local interests.
"We have no idea what Janet Reno is going to do but we think it is a spurious argument that they're making," he said.

"The concentration of ownership that they're talking about.... is nothing more than a red herring," he added. "There's concentration of ownership everywhere throughout the grain industry and there's no way to avoid it. To think that's going to lead to any wrongdoing is spurious at best."
